title: “BECAUSE YOU ARE LUKEWARM, I WILL SPIT YOU OUT” — THE TERRIFYING TRUTH ABOUT WHAT JESUS REALLY MEANT
paragraphs: “BECAUSE YOU ARE LUKEWARM, I WILL SPIT YOU OUT” — THE TERRIFYING TRUTH ABOUT WHAT JESUS REALLY MEANT

You may have heard this verse preached your entire life. But what if the most frightening part isn't that Jesus threatens to spit the lukewarm out of His mouth… but that the very people He was warning believed they were spiritually rich, perfectly fine, and needed absolutely nothing?
There is something more dangerous than a sinner who knows he is lost.
It is a person who believes he is close to God simply because he has learned how to look like a Christian.
Someone who knows when to say “Amen.”
Someone who shares Bible verses, attends church, listens to worship music, and knows exactly how to sound spiritual when other believers are listening.
But behind closed doors…
Prayer has become an occasional emergency call.
Repentance has become something other people need.
The Bible remains unopened for days.
And Jesus has slowly become someone they acknowledge rather than someone they follow.
The frightening part?
They may not even realize anything is wrong.
Because the most dangerous spiritual condition is not always rebellion that announces itself.
Sometimes it is self-sufficiency dressed in religion.
And nearly two thousand years ago, Jesus spoke directly to a church living in that condition.
Not to pagans in the marketplace.
Not to Roman soldiers.
Not to people who had never heard His name.
To a church.
And His words were so disturbing that generations of Christians have repeated them with trembling:
“So then because thou art lukewarm, and neither cold nor hot, I will spue thee out of my mouth.” — Revelation 3:16, KJV
But here is the question we desperately need to ask.
What did Jesus actually mean by lukewarm?
Was He saying that God prefers someone who openly rejects Him over someone who follows Him imperfectly?
Was He condemning Christians who struggle with temptation, spiritual exhaustion, depression, unanswered prayers, or seasons of weakness?
Was He teaching that unless your emotions burn with spiritual excitement every moment of every day, you are in danger of being rejected?
Or have we sometimes reduced a devastatingly specific warning into a slogan that misses the deeper wound Jesus was exposing?
Because when you understand the city receiving this message, the original Greek words, and the astonishing invitation Jesus gives immediately afterward…
This passage becomes more than a warning.
It becomes a mirror.
And perhaps, for someone reading this right now, it will become the moment they finally stop pretending.
The words appear in Revelation 3:14–22, in a message addressed to the church in Laodicea.
Laodicea was a prosperous city in Roman Asia Minor, in what is now Türkiye.
It was known for its wealth, commercial activity, textile production, and connections to medicine, including eye treatments.
After a devastating earthquake in the first century, ancient accounts describe the city's ability to recover using its own resources.
That detail matters.
Laodicea had money.
Laodicea had influence.
Laodicea had the confidence that comes from being able to provide for itself.
And the church living in that environment was confronted by Jesus with words that exposed the spiritual danger beneath its prosperity.
“Because thou sayest, I am rich, and increased with goods, and have need of nothing…” — Revelation 3:17, KJV
Read that slowly.
I have need of nothing.
Not merely, “I have enough money.”
Not merely, “My business is doing well.”
But a posture of self-sufficiency so deep that the people could no longer recognize their spiritual poverty.
Jesus continued:
“…and knowest not that thou art wretched, and miserable, and poor, and blind, and naked.” — Revelation 3:17, KJV
Imagine hearing those words.
You believe you are wealthy.
Jesus says you are poor.
You believe you can see clearly.
Jesus says you are blind.
You believe you are properly clothed.
Jesus says you are naked.
You believe you need nothing.
Jesus says you do not even recognize your deepest need.
The tragedy of Laodicea was not simply that the church had problems.
Every church has problems.
Every believer is still being sanctified.
The tragedy was that its self-assessment had become almost completely disconnected from Christ's assessment.
And that is where the warning begins to reach into our lives.
Because it is possible to become financially successful while spiritually impoverished.
It is possible to know Christian vocabulary without knowing the Shepherd's voice.
It is possible to defend biblical truth in arguments while resisting that same truth in private.
It is possible to become so comfortable with the appearance of Christianity that we stop asking whether our hearts are actually surrendered to Christ.
And perhaps the most uncomfortable question is not whether we can identify lukewarm Christians around us.
It is whether we have become too confident in our own spiritual condition to recognize what Jesus might be correcting in us.
Now consider the original language.
The Greek word translated lukewarm in Revelation 3:16 is χλιαρός (chliaros).
It means lukewarm or tepid.
Jesus says:
“οὔτε ψυχρὸς εἶ οὔτε ζεστός”
Oute psychros ei oute zestos.
“You are neither cold nor hot.”
And then:
“μέλλω σε ἐμέσαι ἐκ τοῦ στόματός μου”
Mellō se emesai ek tou stomatos mou.
“I am about to vomit you out of My mouth.”
The verb ἐμέσαι (emesai) comes from the Greek verb meaning to vomit.
This is stronger than the polite English word spit might suggest.
Jesus deliberately uses a disturbing physical image.
Something is so objectionable that the response is expulsion from the mouth.
But what makes the image especially interesting is the geography surrounding Laodicea.
Nearby Hierapolis was famous for its hot mineral springs, while Colossae was associated with cold, refreshing water.
Laodicea depended on water brought into the city through an engineered supply system, and ancient water infrastructure and mineral deposits remain part of its archaeological history.
This has led many interpreters to suggest that Jesus was drawing on the familiar contrast between useful hot water, refreshing cold water, and unpleasant tepid water.
Under this interpretation, hot water could serve beneficial purposes, cold water could refresh, and lukewarm water represented something distasteful or ineffective.
That is a compelling explanation.
But biblical honesty requires an important distinction.
The text itself does not explicitly say that Jesus was comparing the water supplies of Hierapolis, Colossae, and Laodicea.
The geographical explanation is a plausible historical interpretation, not a detail directly stated in Revelation.
Scholars have debated how much weight it should carry.
What the passage clearly establishes is that Jesus found the church's present condition unacceptable and that its confident claim to need nothing was profoundly false.
And this corrects a common misunderstanding.
You may have heard someone say:
“God would rather you be completely cold toward Him than halfway committed.”
But we should be careful.

Revelation 3:15 says Jesus wishes the church were either cold or hot. It does not explicitly define cold as hatred of God, nor does it teach that outright unbelief is spiritually preferable to imperfect discipleship.
If the water imagery is intended, both hot and cold can represent something beneficial, while lukewarm represents something objectionable.
Even if someone understands the temperatures differently, the central rebuke remains unmistakable.
Jesus is confronting a church whose spiritual reality contradicts its confidence.
And that should stop us from turning this verse into a weapon against every struggling Christian.
Because there is a difference between a believer who is fighting sin and a person who has made peace with sin.
There is a difference between someone who cries, “Lord, help my unbelief,” and someone who believes they no longer need correction.
There is a difference between spiritual weariness and spiritual complacency.
A Christian who feels exhausted but keeps reaching for Christ is not automatically the lukewarm person Revelation condemns.
A believer who falls, repents, and returns to Jesus is not the same as someone who uses grace as permission to remain unchanged.
The person who whispers through tears, “Jesus, I want to love You more, but I am struggling,” should not hear Revelation 3 as proof that Christ has abandoned them.
Remember the father in Mark 9:24 who cried:
“Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief.”
Jesus did not respond by demanding that the man manufacture perfect confidence before receiving help.
And remember Peter.
Peter promised extraordinary loyalty.
Then, when fear took hold, he denied Jesus three times.
Not once.
Not twice.
Three times.
He stood near a fire, warming himself, while the Savior he claimed to love was being rejected.
Imagine the shame when the rooster crowed.
Imagine remembering every promise.
Imagine realizing that the courage you believed you possessed had collapsed when it mattered most.
Yet after the resurrection, Jesus met Peter again.
In John 21, Christ confronted him with a deeply personal question:
“Lovest thou me?”
And then entrusted him with the responsibility of caring for His sheep.
Peter's failure was real.
His repentance mattered.
But his failure was not the final chapter of his story.
That is the difference grace makes.
Grace does not tell us that denying Jesus is harmless.
Grace tells us that failure does not have to be the end when we return to the risen Savior.
And perhaps someone reading this has been carrying a failure that still feels impossible to escape.
You once prayed with conviction.
You once read Scripture with hunger.
You once believed that you would never compromise certain things.
But life became complicated.
A relationship pulled you away.
A disappointment hardened your heart.
An unanswered prayer left you confused.
A secret habit became a repeated surrender.
You stopped confessing because you were tired of promising to change.
And slowly, without a dramatic announcement, your spiritual life became something you maintained in public while neglecting in private.
You still believe in Jesus.
But you know there are rooms in your heart where you have resisted His authority.
And this is where Revelation refuses to let us hide behind either religious performance or hopeless shame.
Because the same Jesus who says, “I will spit you out,” also says something astonishing.
“As many as I love, I rebuke and chasten: be zealous therefore, and repent.” — Revelation 3:19, KJV
Do not rush past those first words.
As many as I love.
The warning is severe.
The call to repentance is urgent.
But Jesus explicitly connects His rebuke to His love.
The Greek text says:
“ἐγὼ ὅσους ἐὰν φιλῶ ἐλέγχω καὶ παιδεύω”
Egō hosous ean philō elenchō kai paideuō.
“Those whom I love, I reprove and discipline.”
The verb φιλῶ (philō) expresses love or affection.
The verb ἐλέγχω (elenchō) concerns exposing, reproving, or correcting.
And παιδεύω (paideuō) carries the sense of discipline, training, or correction.
Jesus is not describing a sentimental love that refuses to confront what destroys us.
He is describing love that tells the truth.
Love that exposes deception.
Love that calls people away from self-destruction.
Love that refuses to affirm spiritual blindness simply because honesty might feel uncomfortable.
Sometimes the most merciful thing Jesus can do is disturb the peace we have made with sin.
Not because He delights in humiliating us.
But because a comfortable lie can keep us from seeking the only One who can save us.
And notice what Jesus commands next.
“Be zealous therefore, and repent.”
The Greek word translated repent is μετανόησον (metanoēson), an imperative form of metanoeō.
It calls for repentance—a genuine change of mind and heart that turns a person away from sin and toward God.
Biblical repentance is not merely feeling guilty after being exposed.
It is not crying for a few minutes and then deliberately returning to the same rebellion without concern.
It is not posting a spiritual quote to compensate for a private life we refuse to surrender.
Repentance involves turning toward Christ in faith and allowing His truth to confront the direction of our lives.
And genuine repentance bears fruit.
Not because good works purchase salvation.
But because saving grace does not leave us indifferent to the Savior.
Ephesians 2:8–10 makes the relationship clear.
We are saved by grace through faith, not by works.
Yet we are created in Christ Jesus for good works.
The works do not buy the grace.
The grace produces a transformed life.
And this matters enormously.
Because if you read Revelation 3 and conclude, “I must become impressive enough for Jesus to accept me,” you have misunderstood the Gospel.
Jesus is not selling salvation to the most emotionally passionate Christians.
He is calling self-sufficient sinners to recognize their need and receive from Him what they cannot provide for themselves.
Listen to what He tells Laodicea:

“I counsel thee to buy of me gold tried in the fire, that thou mayest be rich; and white raiment, that thou mayest be clothed… and anoint thine eyes with eyesalve, that thou mayest see.” — Revelation 3:18, KJV
Think about the tenderness and precision of this invitation.
To a wealthy city, Jesus offers true riches.
To a city associated with textiles, He offers garments that cover spiritual nakedness.
To a place connected with eye treatments, He offers the sight its people desperately lack.
Their greatest strengths had become illustrations of their deepest needs.
They had resources.
But they needed Christ.
They had clothing.
But they needed His righteousness.
They had remedies for physical eyes.
But they needed spiritual sight.
And here is the uncomfortable question.
What if the very thing that makes you feel secure is the thing that has helped you forget your dependence on God?
Your income?
Your reputation?
Your ministry?
Your biblical knowledge?
Your years of church attendance?
Your ability to quote Scripture faster than someone else?
Your position in a Christian community?
None of these things is inherently evil.
But none of them can replace Jesus.
You can be surrounded by religious activity and still need to repent.
You can serve in a ministry while secretly neglecting communion with Christ.
You can become skilled at explaining grace while struggling to receive it with humility.
And you can spend so much time examining everyone else's spiritual temperature that you never allow the Word of God to examine your own heart.
Perhaps that is why the message to Laodicea is so enduring.
It dismantles the illusion that spiritual health can be measured by outward success.
But now we reach the verse that makes this entire passage almost unbearable in its beauty.
After the rebuke…
After the exposure…
After Jesus describes a church that makes Him want to vomit…
He says:
“Behold, I stand at the door, and knock: if any man hear my voice, and open the door, I will come in to him, and will sup with him, and he with me.” — Revelation 3:20, KJV
Stop there.
Read it again.
Jesus is knocking.
The One who knows their condition.
The One who has exposed their poverty.
The One who has called them to repentance.
He is still inviting them to fellowship.
The Greek begins:
“Ἰδοὺ ἕστηκα ἐπὶ τὴν θύραν καὶ κρούω”
Idou hestēka epi tēn thyran kai krouō.
“Behold, I stand at the door and knock.”
The verb ἕστηκα (hestēka) is a perfect-tense form of the verb meaning to stand, conveying a present standing condition.
And κρούω (krouō) means I knock.
The picture is vivid.
Christ stands at the door and calls for a response.
Importantly, this verse was originally addressed to a church, not written primarily as a generic formula for inviting Jesus into one's heart.
Its immediate context is Christ's call for a compromised congregation to repent and be restored to fellowship with Him.
Yet the invitation is deeply personal.
“If any man hear my voice…”
Not merely if the congregation changes its reputation.
Not merely if the church becomes more impressive.
If anyone hears.
One person.
One responding heart.
And the promise is fellowship.
“I will come in to him, and will sup with him, and he with me.”
In the ancient world, sharing a meal was an expression of hospitality, relationship, and communion.
Jesus is offering more than an improved religious image.
He is offering restored fellowship with Himself.
The Savior who exposes the truth also extends the invitation.
And that should break something open inside us.
Because we often imagine that if Jesus saw everything, He would immediately turn away.
But He already sees everything.
The envy you never confessed.
The bitterness you keep defending.
The private compromise.
The spiritual pride.
The prayerlessness.
The fear.
The exhaustion.
The ways you have tried to satisfy your soul with things that cannot save it.
He sees it all.
And His call is not, “Pretend you are better.”
It is, “Repent.”
Come into the light.
Stop defending what is destroying you.
Stop confusing religious appearances with spiritual life.
Stop trying to purchase with performance what only grace can provide.
And come to Christ.
Because the Gospel is not the story of morally impressive people climbing their way into God's acceptance.
It is the story of Jesus Christ coming to rescue sinners who could never rescue themselves.
The eternal Son of God took on flesh.
He lived in perfect obedience to the Father.
He bore our sins on the cross.
He died.
He was buried.
And on the third day, He rose again.
His resurrection is not merely an inspirational ending to a tragic story.
It is the victory of the living Savior over sin and death.
And everyone who truly turns to Him in repentance and faith finds mercy that cannot be earned by religious performance.
That does not make holiness optional.
It makes holiness the fruit of belonging to Him.
Jesus does not save us so we can comfortably worship the sins that nailed Him to the cross.
He saves us to reconcile us to God and transform us into His likeness.
And transformation is not always dramatic.
Sometimes it looks like opening the Bible again after months of neglect.
Sometimes it looks like confessing a hidden sin to God and seeking accountable, trustworthy help.
Sometimes it looks like apologizing without defending yourself.
Sometimes it looks like deleting what repeatedly leads you into temptation.
Sometimes it looks like choosing integrity when nobody would discover the compromise.
Sometimes it looks like praying through tears when you have no idea what to say.
And sometimes it looks like admitting the sentence your pride has avoided for years:
“Jesus, I need You.”
Not just for heaven someday.
Not just when life becomes unbearable.
Today.
In my decisions.
In my relationships.
In my finances.
In my ambitions.
In my habits.
In the places where I have resisted Your Word.
I need You.
That is not weakness to be ashamed of.
That is the beginning of spiritual honesty.
And perhaps you have spent years believing that the opposite of lukewarm Christianity is constant emotional intensity.
You thought you needed louder worship.
More tears.
More religious activity.
More visible enthusiasm.
But emotional intensity alone is not the measure of faithfulness.
A person can shout during worship and still refuse to forgive.
A person can cry at the altar and still deliberately nurture dishonesty.
A person can speak passionately about Jesus while treating people with cruelty.
And a person can quietly care for a sick parent, resist temptation, pray faithfully, love difficult neighbors, and obey Christ without ever becoming publicly impressive.
The question is not simply, “How excited do I feel?”
The deeper question is, “Am I trusting Christ, listening to His Word, repenting when confronted, and learning to obey Him?”
Because spiritual life is not measured by how convincing we look to an audience.
It is measured by our relationship to the living Christ, whose grace bears fruit in our lives.
You do not need to describe your private sins publicly.
But perhaps you can make a simple, honest declaration.
Not because a comment saves you.
Not because public engagement proves repentance.
But because sometimes the first visible step toward renewed fellowship is admitting that we need prayer, truth, and the encouragement of the body of Christ.
And if you are reading this while feeling deeply convicted, remember something essential.
Conviction should lead you toward repentance and Christ, not into endless despair.
Romans 8:1 declares:
“There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus.”
This is not permission to remain unrepentant.
It is the assurance that those who belong to Christ are not required to live under the hopeless verdict of their past.
There is forgiveness.
There is cleansing.
There is restoration.
There is grace.
Not cheap grace that pretends sin is harmless.
Costly grace, purchased through the sacrifice of Jesus Christ.
Grace that forgives.
Grace that teaches.
Grace that disciplines.
Grace that restores.
Grace that transforms.
And perhaps this is where the words “From Scandal to Grace” become more than a beautiful phrase.
Because Peter's denial was scandalous.
The woman caught in adultery in John 8 stood publicly exposed, and Jesus confronted both her accusers and the reality of her sin.
The prodigal son disgraced himself in a distant country, only to discover that his father was ready to receive his return.
And Paul, once a persecutor of Christians, became a witness to the grace of the risen Christ.
Their stories were not identical.
Their circumstances were different.
But each reminds us that sin, shame, and failure do not have to possess the final word when God's redeeming grace intervenes.
Jesus does not rewrite our history by pretending our sins never happened.
He rewrites the future of those He redeems by forgiving their guilt, reconciling them to God, and transforming the direction of their lives.
Not because scandal was beautiful.
But because the Savior is merciful.
And if Christ can restore Peter, forgive sinners, and transform persecutors into servants of the Gospel, then do not assume your own story is beyond His reach.
But do not use His mercy as an excuse to delay repentance.
The invitation is precious precisely because it must be taken seriously.
Revelation 3 does not end with Jesus merely knocking.
It ends with a promise to the one who overcomes, followed by a call to listen:
“He that hath an ear, let him hear what the Spirit saith unto the churches.” — Revelation 3:22, KJV
That includes us.
Not because we are ancient Laodiceans.
But because the Word of God still confronts the human heart.
And our generation has its own forms of spiritual self-sufficiency.
We can accumulate information without wisdom.
Followers without discipleship.
Religious content without prayer.
Online arguments without love.
Christian merchandise without Christian character.
Public declarations without private obedience.
We can build an entire digital identity around Jesus while neglecting the actual teachings of Jesus.
And that possibility should sober every Christian content creator, every ministry leader, and every believer—including us at Gospel Warrior.
Because this warning is not something we get to preach at everyone else while placing ourselves above it.
We need it too.
We need the Word to correct us.
We need accountability.
We need humility.
We need the Holy Spirit's work in our lives.
We need the Gospel we proclaim.
And we never want Gospel Warrior to become another place where people merely consume emotional religious content and then walk away unchanged.
We want these words to send you back to Scripture.
Back to prayer.
Back to your local church and faithful Christian fellowship.
Back to the hard, beautiful work of discipleship.
Back to Jesus.
That is why sharing this message matters.
Somewhere on your Facebook friends list is a person who still appears spiritually strong but is quietly drifting.
Someone who has not prayed honestly in months.
Someone who feels ashamed of how far they have wandered.
Someone who believes God could never receive them again.
Someone who has confused religious activity with a surrendered life.
And someone who has been wounded by the careless misuse of this very passage.
Not to embarrass anyone.
Not to announce that your friends are lukewarm.
But to place a biblically grounded invitation to repentance, grace, and restoration where someone might encounter it at the moment they need it.
His invitation matters too.
Invite your family, your Christian friends, those who have drifted from faith, and even those who are still exploring who Jesus really is.
Because the goal is not merely to gather an audience.
It is to help people encounter the truth of the Gospel and grow in faithful discipleship.
And if these articles have strengthened your walk with Christ, there is another meaningful way to participate in this mission.
For believers who choose to give as an expression of generosity and stewardship, that support can be a meaningful part of their Christian giving.
Scripture teaches in 2 Corinthians 9:7 that giving should not be reluctant or compelled, because God loves a cheerful giver.
We will never tell you that you must pay us to glorify God.
You can glorify Him through obedience, prayer, generosity, service, faithful stewardship, and love for your neighbor.
These products are not the heart of the ministry.
Jesus is.
The resources are simply tools that can help keep biblical encouragement, learning, and discipleship present in everyday life.
We want the Word of God to remain accessible.
We want struggling Christians to find biblical encouragement.
We want new believers to have resources for spiritual growth.
We want families to discover materials that help them talk about Jesus together.
And we want the message of repentance, forgiveness, redemption, and transformation through Christ to travel far beyond the reach of any single article.
Not out of fear.
Not because God needs your money.
But because, if this mission reflects your convictions and you are able to give, your generosity can help make more biblical discipleship resources available to others.
Pray for the people these messages reach.
Invite others to read the Bible for themselves.
Speak about Jesus with patience and truth.
And live the Gospel you profess.
Because in the end, the most important thing about this article is not how many people read it.
It is whether we hear what Christ is saying.
Perhaps tonight, after the phone is placed on the table and the noise of the day finally disappears, you will sit quietly with an open Bible.
Perhaps you will read Revelation 3:14–22 for yourself.
Perhaps you will notice the words you have heard so many times and suddenly understand them differently.
Not as an invitation to panic every time your emotions feel weak.
Not as permission to condemn struggling believers.
Not as a threat that can be escaped through religious performance.
But as a solemn warning against self-sufficient, unrepentant Christianity—and a gracious invitation to return to the One who alone can make us spiritually rich.
Maybe your prayer will not be eloquent.
Maybe it will be only a few words.
“Lord Jesus, show me what I cannot see about myself.”
“Forgive me for the ways I have trusted my own righteousness.”
“Teach me to repent without making excuses.”
“Restore my hunger for Your Word.”
“Help me follow You when no one is watching.”
“Make my life a reflection of Your grace.”
That prayer will not make you impressive in the eyes of the world.
But spiritual renewal has never depended on impressing the world.
It begins with the mercy of God and a heart that responds to His truth.
And before you leave this article, there is one final question worth carrying into the silence.
When Jesus says, “You do not know that you are poor, blind, and naked,” are you willing to let Him reveal the things you have been unwilling to see?
Because the real danger is not discovering that you need repentance.
The danger is becoming so satisfied with yourself that you no longer believe you need it.
And the real hope is not that you can somehow manufacture enough spiritual heat to make yourself acceptable to God.
The hope is Jesus Christ Himself.
The crucified and risen Savior.
The One who exposes our sin without being deceived by our appearances.
The One who calls us to repent.
The One who offers forgiveness and fellowship.
The One who is worthy of our trust, our obedience, our worship, and our lives.
And if all you can say today is “Christ is still healing me,” that is a meaningful place to begin a conversation and ask for prayer.
But whatever you do, do not let the comment become a substitute for the conversation you need to have with God.
The screen will go dark.
The notifications will stop.
The world will move on to another story.
But the words of Jesus will remain.
The most frightening thing about being lukewarm is believing you need nothing. The most beautiful thing about grace is discovering that Jesus is everything you need.
